Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. ## Quick start **[Get started at rea.tools](https://rea.tools/get-started/)** for step-by-step instructions by operating system, agent, and analysis provider. ### Connect your agent (MCP) With [Node.js and npm](docs/reference/supported-targets.md) installed, run this from a trusted directory outside the project you plan to analyze. ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agent, review and approve the setup plan, then restart your agent. Setup backs up existing configuration and adds REA's MCP connection and investigation skill. See the [installation guide](docs/getting-started/installation.md) for supported clients, plugins, manual registration, and troubleshooting. Try asking your agent: ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use REA from the terminal (CLI) Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. The [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/getting-started/cli.md) covers provider selection, native commands, snapshots, and scripting. For Linux prerequisites, see the [installation guide](docs/getting-started/installation.md#linux-owned-process-prerequisite). ### Update REA For a global npm or Bun installation, run the updater and follow its setup instructions. ```bash rea update ``` If you use `npx`, refresh your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. See [update and uninstall instructions](docs/getting-started/installation.md#diagnose-update-and-remove) for package runner options and troubleshooting. ## Showcases

DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation

Recover a position-to-pan helper from x86 instructions and verify the C reconstruction against 3,205 original-x86 cases and all 63 compiled function bytes.

Read the case study · Reconstruction repository

Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge

Follow the renderer’s clipboard API through preload and IPC into the main process to see how Notion handles rich clipboard data.

Read the case study

TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation

Recover fixed and aimed angle calculations from the PC-98 game’s 16-bit instructions and compare the reconstructed C++ with historical compiler output.

Read the case study · Reconstruction repository
If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an [issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) or a [pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls), including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found. ## How REA works Your agent uses REA through MCP to inspect a target and trace the relevant code. It can use the evidence REA returns to ask follow-up questions, explain behavior, or build and test an implementation. The CLI uses the same workflows. [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA covers native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, websites, .NET assemblies, Android apps, firmware, and recorded runtime and network activity. [Supported targets and requirements](docs/reference/supported-targets.md) For native decompilation, choose a provider that supports your target format and host OS. See [choosing a deep analysis provider](docs/reference/supported-targets.md#choosing-a-deep-analysis-provider). ## Build RL environments Build a local environment from a recorded web session or a Linux desktop app so an agent can practice a task and check its result. [Build an RL environment with REA](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/). ## FAQ
Which agents can use REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the [supported agents](docs/getting-started/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use [manual MCP registration](docs/getting-started/installation.md#mcp-registry).
Do I need a native analysis engine? Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md#hopper) for the options and their supported targets.
Do I need to start Hopper first? REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See [Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).
What does installing the skill from skills.sh do? The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/getting-started/installation.md#skill-only-installation).
What code does REA return? Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.
Does REA upload my app? REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` For agent setup through `npx`: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.
## Documentation Start with the website's [worked guides](https://rea.tools/guides/). For exact options, prerequisites and result contracts: - [Installation and setup](docs/getting-started/installation.md): agent registration, provider configuration, updates and uninstall. - [Readiness and troubleshooting](docs/getting-started/installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task): diagnose one agent or analysis engine. - [CLI and Evidence](docs/getting-started/cli.md): commands, provider selection, snapshots, import/export and exit statuses. - [MCP contracts](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md) and [agent prompts](docs/getting-started/mcp-prompts.md): tool results, sessions and guided investigations. - [Tool catalog](docs/reference/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog): generated inventory of tools, providers and CLI commands. releases.body:
## [6.9.0](https://github.com/morluto/rea/compare/rea-agents-6.8.0...rea-agents-6.9.0) (2026-11-11)

### Highlights

- Build and test desktop tasks from recorded application state, including downloaded Linux apps, reusable build computers and multiple tasks per capture.
- Inspect more shipped artifacts offline: standalone application bundles, embedded firmware, NTFS acquisitions, API contracts and V8 code-cache containers.
- Keep native and runtime investigations grounded in retained Evidence, with paged results, explicit coverage and recoverable resource limits.

### Changes

- Analyze targets and create private runtimes on fixed local ReFS volumes as well as NTFS, preserving persistent ACL, file identity, snapshot and cleanup checks. [#10086](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pull/10086). Thanks @QianNangong.
- Capture, export and witness desktop tasks inside a build computer; keep an agentenv computer available through MCP and prepare a build host from one command. releases.body:
## [6.8.0](https://github.com/morluto/rea/compare/rea-agents-6.7.0...rea-agents-6.8.0) (2026-10-25)

### Highlights

- Build local agent environments from network captures, browser scenarios, or a prompt, then serve derived reads and evidence-gated writes and compare them with fresh application captures.
- Inspect more shipped formats, including GPU code objects, BEAM, Python bytecode, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK, PyInstaller, Node.js SEA, devicetree, and additional PE/ELF tables.
- Keep large investigations focused with retained summaries, selected fact queries, configurable recovery limits, and row-oriented CLI exports. Complete Evidence remains available.

### ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

- **Function analysis:** `analyze_function` now defaults to a retained summary. Set `detail: "complete"` for the previous inline dossier; the CLI retains its complete default and requires `--evidence_output` when selecting a summary. [#5660](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pull/5660). Thanks @CryptoJones, @gensokyo-dev, @RishTheFish21.

releases.body:
## [6.7.0](https://github.com/morluto/rea/compare/rea-agents-6.6.0...rea-agents-6.7.0) (2026-10-18)

### Highlights

- Client configuration edits follow the duplicate-member semantics used by MCP clients.

### Changes

- Includes the [6.6.0 changes and migration notes](https://github.com/morluto/rea/releases/tag/rea-agents-6.6.0). That version was tagged but was not published to npm.

### Fixes

- **Client configuration:** Setup edits the last repeated JSON/JSONC member, matching the value clients actually read. Setup and uninstall refuse a removal that would reactivate a shadowed duplicate, preserving the original configuration. ([#4957](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pull/4957), [morluto/rea#4952](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues/4952)). Thanks @kaoru0822-kitauji, @xu91102.

For a global npm or Bun installation, run the updater and follow its setup instructions.

If you use npx, refresh your agent setup with:

Review the setup changes and restart your agent. See update and uninstall instructions for package runner options and troubleshooting.

How REA works

Your agent uses REA through MCP to inspect a target and trace the relevant code. It can use the evidence REA returns to ask follow-up questions, explain behavior, or build and test an implementation. The CLI uses the same workflows.

FAQ

Which agents can use REA?

Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the supported agents; other clients can use manual MCP registration.

Do I need a native analysis engine?

Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See provider setup for the options and their supported targets.

Do I need to start Hopper first?

REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See Hopper startup and troubleshooting.

The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use npx rea-agents setup to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See skill-only installation.

Does REA upload my app?

What should I do if I hit a bug?

Update first; a recent release may already fix it.

For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global:

rea update

For agent setup through npx:

npx rea-agents@latest setup

If you're using an agent, complete the setup refresh and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, open an issue with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.

Community & Support

  • Discord — Ask questions and share what you’re investigating with our passionate community of over 50,000 reverse engineers and builders!
  • Twitter / X — Follow @reatools for updates and announcements.
  • Feedback & Ideas — Want a new feature or support for a file format? Open a GitHub issue or join our Discord and let us know.

🎉 400,000 GitHub stars — thank you!

Contributing

We'd love your help with REA! Open an issue to report a bug or suggest a feature, or send a pull request to improve the code or docs.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and checks. See the testing guide for verification lanes.

Disclaimer

See DISCLAIMER.md for responsible-use guidance.

The project's position on illegal or unauthorized use covers all REA versions, distribution channels, and platforms; each copy retains its applicable licenses.

REA is for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you own or are authorized to examine.

aiSummary.oneLiner: Universal reverse engineering client for binaries, applications, and runtime behavior using the Model Context Protocol.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: REA provides a unified interface for analyzing compiled binaries and application runtime behavior without switching contexts. It connects to various reverse engineering tools and plugins via the Model Context Protocol to extract and interpret execution traces and memory dumps. The system allows seamless navigation from high-level application features down to specific machine instructions. By integrating multiple analytical backends, it eliminates the need to manually coordinate separate decompilers, debuggers, and static analysis utilities.
keyFeatures: Cross-tool protocol: Integrates diverse reverse engineering tools using the Model Context Protocol.
Binary analysis: Provides deep inspection capabilities for compiled executables across different architectures.
Runtime tracing: Captures and analyzes dynamic execution behavior directly from running applications.
Unified interface: Merges static and dynamic analysis workflows into a single cohesive client experience.
Extensible backend: Supports adding new disassemblers and debuggers via standardized plugins.

useCases.title: Vulnerability Research
useCases.description: Analyze compiled binaries to discover memory corruption flaws and logical vulnerabilities.

useCases.title: Malware Analysis
useCases.description: Safely inspect malicious payloads to understand their runtime behavior and network callbacks.

useCases.title: Protocol Reverse Engineering
useCases.description: Deconstruct undocumented binary protocols by tracing how the application serializes data.

useCases.title: Legacy Code Maintenance
useCases.description: Understand the inner workings of legacy systems where source code is no longer available.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Security researchers, vulnerability analysts, and reverse engineers who need to analyze compiled binaries and complex runtime environments. Users should be familiar with assembly language, debuggers, and low-level system architecture.
